claim: HIV-1 infects multiple bone marrow cell types.
source: HIV-1 infects multiple BM cell types, but virus dissemination within BM has been poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about HIV-1 infection in bone marrow.

claim: Tissue clearing combined with confocal and light sheet fluorescence microscopy revealed distinct populations of HIV-1 p24-producing cells in bone marrow early after infection.
source: Tissue clearing combined with confocal and light sheet fluorescence microscopy revealed distinct populations of HIV-1 p24-producing cells in BM early after infection
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's imaging experiments.

claim: Macrophages are the principal subset of virus-producing cells in bone marrow over time.
source: quantification of these populations identified macrophages as the principal subset of virus-producing cells in BM over time.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: HIV-1 dissemination in bone marrow occurs through semi-synchronous budding from T-cell and macrophage membranes.
source: Electron tomography demonstrated three modes of HIV-1 dissemination in BM: (i) semi-synchronous budding from T-cell and macrophage membranes
evidence: This is a primary finding from electron tomography experiments.

claim: Mature virus associates with virus-producing T-cell uropods contacting putative target cells.
source: Electron tomography demonstrated three modes of HIV-1 dissemination in BM: (i) semi-synchronous budding from T-cell and macrophage membranes, (ii) mature virus association with virus-producing T-cell uropods contacting putative target cells
evidence: This is a primary finding from electron tomography experiments.

claim: Macrophages engulf HIV-1-producing T-cells and produce virus within enclosed intracellular compartments that fuse to invaginations with access to the extracellular space.
source: Electron tomography demonstrated three modes of HIV-1 dissemination in BM: (i) semi-synchronous budding from T-cell and macrophage membranes, (ii) mature virus association with virus-producing T-cell uropods contacting putative target cells, and (iii) macrophages engulfing HIV-1–producing T-cells and producing virus within enclosed intracellular compartments that fused to invaginations with access to the extracellular space.
evidence: This is a primary finding from electron tomography experiments.

claim: Bone marrow functions as both a primary and secondary lymphoid organ.
source: Bone marrow (BM) within the spongy matrix of long bones functions as both a primary and secondary lymphoid organ and is the main site for hematopoiesis of immune cells destined for tissues throughout the body.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bone marrow function.

claim: Bone marrow is the main site for hematopoiesis of immune cells destined for tissues throughout the body.
source: Bone marrow (BM) within the spongy matrix of long bones functions as both a primary and secondary lymphoid organ and is the main site for hematopoiesis of immune cells destined for tissues throughout the body.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bone marrow function.

claim: Bone marrow contains CD4+ T-cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells commonly associated with HIV-1 pathogenesis.
source: It contains cells commonly associated with HIV-1 pathogenesis (e.g., CD4+ T-cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells)
evidence: This is established knowledge about bone marrow cell composition.

claim: Megakaryocytes and committed lymphoid and myeloid progenitor cells in bone marrow are permissive to HIV-1 infection.
source: BM-specific cells such as megakaryocytes and committed lymphoid and myeloid progenitor cells that are also permissive to HIV-1 infection (Alexaki and Wigdahl, 2008; Allen and Dexter, 1984; Folks et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HIV-1 infection leads to abnormalities in hematopoiesis.
source: HIV-1 infection leads to abnormalities in hematopoiesis (Redd et al., 2007; Thiebot et al., 2001; Yamakami et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Virus replication can be detected in the bone marrow of SIV-infected non-human primates within days after infection.
source: virus replication can be detected in the BM of SIV-infected non-human primates (NHPs) within days after infection (Mandell et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research in non-human primates.

claim: Hematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow can differentiate into multiple HIV-1 permissive cell types that retain the capacity to enter the bloodstream and travel to distant tissue sites.
source: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in BM can differentiate into multiple HIV-1 permissive cell types that retain the capacity to enter the bloodstream and travel to distant tissue sites in a controlled fashion (Geissmann et al., 2010; Pabst, 2018; Pittet et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The process of bone marrow cell migration could facilitate systemic virus dissemination.
source: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in BM can differentiate into multiple HIV-1 permissive cell types that retain the capacity to enter the bloodstream and travel to distant tissue sites in a controlled fashion (Geissmann et al., 2010; Pabst, 2018; Pittet et al., 2014), a process that could facilitate systemic virus dissemination.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the migration capacity of bone marrow cells.

claim: Hematopoietic stem cells and progenitor cells contribute to the HIV-1 virus reservoir.
source: the proposed implication of HSCs and progenitor cells (HSPCs) as cell types that contribute to the virus reservoir (Carter et al., 2011; Carter et al., 2010; McNamara et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Humanized mice are a cost-effective model for imaging HIV-1 within tissues.
source: Humanized mice (hu-mice) are a cost-effective model for imaging HIV-1 within tissues and the only HIV-1 infection from which one can routinely obtain BM from long bone samples.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the humanized mouse model.

claim: Humanized mice are the only HIV-1 infection model from which one can routinely obtain bone marrow from long bone samples.
source: Humanized mice (hu-mice) are a cost-effective model for imaging HIV-1 within tissues and the only HIV-1 infection from which one can routinely obtain BM from long bone samples.
evidence: This is a statement about the unique utility of the humanized mouse model for bone marrow studies.

claim: Studies in HIV-1-infected humanized mice have recapitulated and advanced important observations of HIV-1 disease, including acute spread and systemic dissemination, latency, and target cell depletion.
source: Studies in HIV-1–infected hu-mice have recapitulated and advanced important observations of HIV-1 disease, including acute spread and systemic dissemination, latency, and target cell depletion (Marsden and Zack, 2015; Marsden and Zack, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: BLT humanized mice contain the most complete repertoire of human immune cells of humanized mouse models.
source: Several hu-mouse models have been used to study HIV-1 pathogenesis, with BM, liver, thymus (BLT) hu-mice arguably containing the most complete repertoire of human immune cells of hu-mouse models (Denton and Garcia, 2012; Marsden and Zack, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: BLT mice are created by transplanting human liver and thymus tissues together with autologous CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells into NOD/SCID/IL2Rγ null (NSG) mice.
source: BLT mice are individually created by transplanting human liver and thymus tissues together with autologous CD34+ HSCs into NOD/SCID/IL2Rγ null (NSG) mice.
evidence: This describes the method for creating BLT mice.

claim: Bone marrow from HIV-1-infected BLT humanized mice includes human immune cells that produce virus transcripts during infection.
source: Importantly, BM from HIV-1–infected BLT hu-mice includes human immune cells that produce virus transcripts during infection (Denton et al., 2008; Nixon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tissue clearing methods render samples effectively transparent by removing lipids and other biomolecules to enhance light penetration into the tissue.
source: Larger volume imaging (mm3-cm3) is possible using tissue clearing methods, which render samples effectively transparent by removing lipids and other biomolecules to enhance light penetration into the tissue (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015; Tainaka et al., 2016; Treweek and Gradinaru, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on tissue clearing methods.

claim: Combining tissue clearing with light sheet fluorescence microscopy allows in situ interrogation of large tissue volumes with single cell resolution.
source: Combining tissue clearing with light sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) allows in situ interrogation of large tissue volumes with single cell resolution and rapid generation of quantifiable spatial information that would be difficult to achieve with traditional immunohistochemistry techniques (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015; Tainaka et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tissue clearing has allowed imaging of brain connectivity in mice.
source: Tissue clearing has allowed imaging of brain connectivity in mice (Chung et al., 2013; Susaki et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tissue clearing has allowed imaging of whole-body metastasis in mouse models of cancer.
source: whole-body metastasis in mouse models of cancer (Guldner et al., 2016; Kubota et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tissue clearing has allowed imaging of the distribution of HIV-1-infected cells within gut-associated lymphoid tissue and spleen.
source: the distribution of HIV-1–infected cells within gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) and spleen (Kieffer et al., 2017a; Kieffer et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The inherent density of bone prevents adequate clarification using many tissue clearing techniques.
source: Although the inherent density of bone prevents adequate clarification using many tissue clearing techniques, BM imaging is possible using Bone CLARITY
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of tissue clearing for bone.

claim: Bone CLARITY was developed to clear mouse femurs in order to address the spatial distribution of specific cell populations.
source: BM imaging is possible using Bone CLARITY, which was developed to clear mouse femurs in order to address the spatial distribution of specific cell populations (Greenbaum et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Electron tomography allows 3D visualization of tissue volumes at ultrastructural resolution.
source: Lymphoid tissues can be imaged at higher resolution using electron microscopy (EM), with electron tomography (ET) allowing 3D visualization of tissue volumes at ultrastructural resolution (McIntosh et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Previous electron tomography studies revealed 3D profiles of free and budding HIV-1 virions in humanized mouse gut-associated lymphoid tissue and spleen.
source: These studies revealed 3D profiles of free and budding HIV-1 virions and documented large pools of extracellular cell-free virions localized between cells and occasional instances of virological synapses, supporting roles for both cell-free and cell-to-cell virus dissemination in these hu-mouse tissues (Kieffer et al., 2017b; Ladinsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous electron tomography studies documented large pools of extracellular cell-free HIV-1 virions localized between cells in humanized mouse gut-associated lymphoid tissue and spleen.
source: These studies revealed 3D profiles of free and budding HIV-1 virions and documented large pools of extracellular cell-free virions localized between cells and occasional instances of virological synapses, supporting roles for both cell-free and cell-to-cell virus dissemination in these hu-mouse tissues (Kieffer et al., 2017b; Ladinsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous electron tomography studies found occasional instances of virological synapses in humanized mouse gut-associated lymphoid tissue and spleen.
source: These studies revealed 3D profiles of free and budding HIV-1 virions and documented large pools of extracellular cell-free virions localized between cells and occasional instances of virological synapses, supporting roles for both cell-free and cell-to-cell virus dissemination in these hu-mouse tissues (Kieffer et al., 2017b; Ladinsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous electron tomography studies support roles for both cell-free and cell-to-cell HIV-1 dissemination in humanized mouse gut-associated lymphoid tissue and spleen.
source: These studies revealed 3D profiles of free and budding HIV-1 virions and documented large pools of extracellular cell-free virions localized between cells and occasional instances of virological synapses, supporting roles for both cell-free and cell-to-cell virus dissemination in these hu-mouse tissues (Kieffer et al., 2017b; Ladinsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Electron tomography studies of murine leukemia virus in secondary lymphoid mouse tissues showed extensive zones of contact between infected macrophages and B-cells.
source: In contrast, our ET studies of murine leukemia virus (MLV) in secondary lymphoid mouse tissues showed extensive zones of contact between infected macrophages and B-cells, virions in the cell-cell interface (virological synapses), and transfer of virions from infected donor cells to uninfected target cells via uropod extensions (Sewald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Electron tomography studies of murine leukemia virus in secondary lymphoid mouse tissues showed virions in the cell-cell interface (virological synapses).
source: In contrast, our ET studies of murine leukemia virus (MLV) in secondary lymphoid mouse tissues showed extensive zones of contact between infected macrophages and B-cells, virions in the cell-cell interface (virological synapses), and transfer of virions from infected donor cells to uninfected target cells via uropod extensions (Sewald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Electron tomography studies of murine leukemia virus in secondary lymphoid mouse tissues showed transfer of virions from infected donor cells to uninfected target cells via uropod extensions.
source: In contrast, our ET studies of murine leukemia virus (MLV) in secondary lymphoid mouse tissues showed extensive zones of contact between infected macrophages and B-cells, virions in the cell-cell interface (virological synapses), and transfer of virions from infected donor cells to uninfected target cells via uropod extensions (Sewald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: BLT humanized mice were generated by transplantation of human fetal liver-derived CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells via retro-orbital vein plexus injection and transplantation of pieces of human liver and thymus under the mouse kidney capsule in 8-week-old irradiated NSG mice.
source: BLT hu-mice were generated by transplantation of human fetal liver-derived CD34+ HSPCs via retro-orbital vein plexus injection and transplantation of pieces of human liver and thymus under the mouse kidney capsule in 8-week-old irradiated NSG mice.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used to generate BLT mice.

claim: Human multi-lineage hematopoietic cell populations were reconstituted in peripheral blood at 13 weeks post transplantation.
source: Human multi-lineage hematopoietic cell populations (hCD45+ hematopoietic, hCD3+ T-cell, hCD19+ B-cell, hCD4+ T-cell and hCD8+ T-cell) were reconstituted in peripheral blood at 13 weeks post transplantation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: BLT humanized mice were infected with CCR5-tropic HIV-1NFNSX at a dose of 200 ng of p24 gag via retro-orbital vein plexus at 14 weeks.
source: BLT hu-mice were infected with CCR5-tropic HIV-1NFNSX at a dose of 200 ng of p24 gag via retro-orbital vein plexus at 14 weeks.
evidence: This describes the experimental infection protocol.

claim: Animals were euthanized and sternums and femurs were harvested at 5 days, 10 days, 63 days and 92 days post-infection.
source: Animals were euthanized and sternums and femurs were harvested to investigate HIV-1 dissemination in BM at 5 days (n = 1), 10 days (n = 2), 63 days (n = 1) and 92 days (n = 1) post-infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental timeline and is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The hCD4/CD8 ratios in peripheral blood were unaltered at 5 and 10 days post-infection and subsequently declined to low levels.
source: The hCD4/CD8 ratios in peripheral blood were unaltered at 5 and 10 days post-infection and subsequently declined to low levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The HIV-1 viral load in peripheral blood was low at 0 and 5 days post-infection, but rapidly reached greater than 1.25 × 10^5 copies of HIV-1 RNA/mL for all later timepoints.
source: Accordingly, the HIV-1 viral load in peripheral blood was low at 0 (m410) and 5 (m419) days post-infection, but rapidly reached greater than 1.25 × 105 copies of HIV-1 RNA/mL for all later timepoints (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Sternums and femurs from HIV-1-infected BLT humanized mice were fixed and cleared by Bone CLARITY.
source: Sternums and femurs from HIV-1–infected BLT hu-mice were fixed and cleared by Bone CLARITY (Greenbaum et al., 2017) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental method and is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Approximately 1-2 mm regions of cleared sternum containing a central channel of bone marrow were imaged by confocal fluorescence microscopy after immunostaining.
source: ~1–2 mm regions of cleared sternum containing a central channel of BM were imaged by confocal fluorescence microscopy after immunostaining for cell nuclei, HIV-1 p24, human CD4 (hCD4)-expressing cells, and human CD68 (hCD68)-expressing macrophages (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This describes the experimental method and is shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Bone marrow does not contain a dense distribution of cells compared with other lymphoid tissues.
source: Compared with other lymphoid tissues, BM does not contain a dense distribution of cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: HIV-1 p24 co-localized with both hCD4+ and hCD68+ cells in bone marrow.
source: HIV-1 p24+ co-localized with both hCD4+ and hCD68+ cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data.

claim: hCD4+ and hCD68+ cells are present within regions of intact, cleared bone marrow from HIV-infected BLT humanized mice.
source: These results showed that hCD4+ and hCD68+ cells are present within regions of intact, cleared BM from HIV-infected BLT hu-mice
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data.

claim: HIV-1 p24 protein expression is associated with both hCD4+ and hCD68+ cell types in bone marrow.
source: confirmed HIV-1 p24 protein expression associated with both cell types as evidenced by co-staining with HIV-1 p24.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data.

claim: Imaging of a ~5 mm long and ~2 mm diameter region of immunostained femur from a 10 day post-infection humanized mouse showed numerous hCD4+ and hCD68+ cells dispersed throughout the bone marrow but relatively few p24+ cells.
source: Imaging of a ~ 5 mm long and ~2 mm diameter region of immunostained femur from a 10 day post-infection (PI) hu-mouse showed numerous hCD4+ and hCD68+ cells dispersed throughout the BM but relatively few p24+ cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Segmentation and quantification detected 626 per mm³ hCD4+ cells, 766 per mm³ hCD68+ cells, and five per mm³ p24+ cells within the sample volume at 10 days post-infection.
source: Segmentation and quantification to detect the density of the individual cell populations showed that 626 per mm3 hCD4+ cells, 766 per mm3 hCD68+ T-cells, and five per mm3 p24+ cells were present within the sample volume.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data.

claim: Additional timepoints post-infection demonstrated a constant density of hCD68+ cells, a decreased density of hCD4+ cells, and a low density of p24+ cells that increased slightly over time.
source: Additional timepoints PI were imaged and quantified, demonstrating a constant density of hCD68+ cells, a decreased density of hCD4+ cells, and a low density of p24+ cells that increased slightly over time (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The reduction of hCD4+ T-cells in bone marrow is consistent with non-human primate studies showing SIV-induced T-cell depletion in bone marrow.
source: The reduction of hCD4+ T-cells is consistent with NHP studies showing SIV-induced T-cell depletion in BM (Hoang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research in non-human primates.

claim: Co-localization analysis indicated that the majority of p24+ cells were hCD68+, with this level remaining consistent over time.
source: Co-localization analysis indicated that the majority of p24+ cells were hCD68+, with this level remaining consistent over time, whereas the percentage of p24+/hCD4+ cells decreased with time (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The percentage of p24+/hCD4+ cells decreased with time.
source: Co-localization analysis indicated that the majority of p24+ cells were hCD68+, with this level remaining consistent over time, whereas the percentage of p24+/hCD4+ cells decreased with time (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Bone marrow extracted by needle aspiration was contaminated with blood from the vasculature.
source: In direct comparisons of ET imaging of BM obtained by needle aspiration versus after dissection and removal from long bones, we found that BM extracted by needle aspiration was contaminated with blood from the vasculature
evidence: This is based on direct experimental comparisons.

claim: Physiologically-relevant regions of bone marrow distinct from contaminating mature red blood cells could only be obtained at the electron microscopy level by extracting bone marrow samples from long bones.
source: we could only obtain physiologically-relevant regions of BM that were distinct from contaminating mature red blood cells at the EM level by extracting BM samples from long bones (unpublished results).
evidence: This is based on direct experimental comparisons.

claim: Bone marrow tissues were obtained by removing ~1 cm of the sternum bone immediately after the mouse was sacrificed.
source: Specifically, BM tissues were obtained by removing ~1 cm of the sternum bone immediately after the mouse was sacrificed and then placing it in a fixative after which the sternum was opened and intact BM was removed without disruption of the underlying tissue structure.
evidence: This describes the experimental method for bone marrow extraction.

claim: Bone marrow from sternums of HIV-1-infected BLT humanized mice was prepared for electron tomography by prefixation with glutaraldehyde and paraformaldehyde followed by high-pressure freezing and freeze-substitution and resin embedding.
source: BM from sternums of HIV-1–infected BLT hu-mice was prepared for ET by prefixation with glutaraldehyde and paraformaldehyde followed by high-pressure freezing and freeze-substitution (HPF/FS) and resin embedding (Kieffer et al., 2017b; Ladinsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the experimental method for electron tomography sample preparation.

claim: Antibody epitopes on resin-embedded samples are typically destroyed, preventing the use of the same samples for high-resolution electron tomography and immuno-electron microscopy.
source: Although we cannot use the same samples for high-resolution ET and immuno-EM because antibody epitopes on resin-embedded samples are typically destroyed (Ladinsky and Howell, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Many of the cells in bone marrow can be identified by morphology.
source: many of the cells in BM can be identified by morphology as we describe below.
evidence: This is a statement about the ability to identify cells by morphology in electron microscopy.

claim: Uninfected BLT mouse bone marrow was not distinguishable from HIV-1-infected BLT mouse bone marrow in terms of cell density, cell types, or cell morphologies, with the exception of not including budding or free virions.
source: With the exception of not including budding or free virions, uninfected BLT mouse BM was not distinguishable from HIV-1–infected BLT mouse BM in terms of cell density, cell types, or cell morphologies (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Large areas of HIV-1-infected bone marrow were surveyed as electron microscopy overviews comprising 50-500 montaged frames at ~6500x magnification.
source: Large areas of HIV-1–infected BM were surveyed as EM overviews comprising 50–500 montaged frames at ~6500 x magnification (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental method and is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Electron microscopy surveys revealed a diverse array of cell morphologies consistent with cells found in bone marrow, including T-cells, B-cells, macrophages, megakaryocytes, and hematopoietic stem cells/hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells.
source: These surveys revealed a diverse array of cell morphologies consistent with cells found in BM, including T-cells, B-cells, macrophages, megakaryocytes, and HSCs/HSPCs (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy imaging data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The density of cells in humanized mouse bone marrow was relatively low compared with tissues such as gut-associated lymphoid tissue and spleen.
source: Compared with tissues such as GALT and spleen, the density of cells in hu-mouse BM was relatively low, as also found for human BM (Brass, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy imaging data and a citation to previous research on human bone marrow.

claim: T-cells can be distinguished by electron microscopy by their round compact shape, large nucleus, and minimal cytoplasm.
source: By EM, T-cells can be distinguished by their round compact shape, large nucleus, and minimal cytoplasm (Zucker-Franklin, 1975) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cells identified by electron microscopy as T-cells were morphologically similar to hCD4+ cells detected by immunofluorescence within cleared bone marrow.
source: Cells identified by EM as T-cells were morphologically similar to hCD4+ cells detected by IF within cleared BM (Figure 1C; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of electron microscopy and immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 2C.

claim: Cells identified as bone marrow T-cells regularly displayed uropods that formed synaptic contacts with neighboring cells.
source: Cells identified as BM T-cells regularly displayed uropods (cytoplasmic protrusions containing organelles and structures promoting cell adhesion and signaling; Sánchez-Madrid and Serrador, 2009; Sewald et al., 2015) that formed synaptic contacts with neighboring cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,G)
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,G.

claim: Uropods are cytoplasmic protrusions containing organelles and structures promoting cell adhesion and signaling.
source: uropods (cytoplasmic protrusions containing organelles and structures promoting cell adhesion and signaling; Sánchez-Madrid and Serrador, 2009; Sewald et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Uropods forming synaptic contacts with neighboring cells is suggestive of the migration characteristics exhibited by some innate immune cells.
source: suggestive of the migration characteristics exhibited by some innate immune cells (Hind et al., 2016; Lämmermann and Sixt, 2009; Sewald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and is an inference from the observed uropod structures.

claim: Macrophages are larger than T-cells and are characterized by a complex morphology that includes deep surface invaginations, multi-lobed nuclei, and populations of vesicles and granules of varying size and electron density.
source: Macrophages are larger than T-cells and are characterized by a complex morphology that includes deep surface invaginations, multi-lobed nuclei, and populations of vesicles and granules of varying size and electron density (Orenstein, 2007; Orenstein and Wahl, 1999) (Figure 1C; 2D-F).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 2D-F.

claim: Serial-section electron tomography of large 3D volumes demonstrated that individual lobes of nuclei in presumptive macrophages were connected.
source: Although some IF and projection EM images appeared to show multiple nuclei in presumptive macrophages, serial-section ET of large 3D volumes demonstrated that individual lobes of nuclei were connected in the ~25 cells that we examined (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Bone marrow macrophages are not polynuclear; they do not contain multiple separate nuclei.
source: suggesting that BM macrophages are not polynuclear; that is they do not contain multiple separate nuclei.
evidence: This is an inference from electron tomography imaging data.

claim: Immunofluorescence data from cleared bone marrow confirmed that macrophages contain continuous, multi-lobed nuclei.
source: Analogous IF data from cleared BM confirmed these observations by showing continuous, multi-lobed nuclei (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Bone marrow macrophages displayed numerous pseudopods emanating from their surfaces.
source: BM macrophages also displayed numerous pseudopods emanating from their surfaces.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy imaging data.

claim: Macrophage pseudopods could be distinguished from uropods emanating from T-cells in that they were smaller and contained organized cytoskeletal filaments, but lacked membranous organelles.
source: Macrophage pseudopods (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) could be distinguished from uropods emanating from T-cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) in that they were smaller and contained organized cytoskeletal filaments, but lacked membranous organelles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-F.

claim: Uropods were found on macrophages, but more rarely than found on bone marrow T-cells.
source: Uropods were also found on macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), but more rarely than found on BM T-cells.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Virions budding from the plasma membrane were detected by electron tomography as early as 5 days post-infection on cells morphologically identified as T-cells and macrophages.
source: Virions budding from the plasma membrane were detected by ET as early as 5 days PI on cells morphologically identified as T-cells (Figure 3A,B) and macrophages (Figure 3C,D)
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: Virions were often seen budding from the surface of T-cells at points corresponding to narrow regions of underlying cytoplasm.
source: Interestingly, virions were often seen budding from the surface of T-cells at points corresponding to narrow regions of underlying cytoplasm (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Virus components and associated host machinery can assemble in a space-limited environment and/or the morphology of HIV-1-infected cells is dynamic.
source: suggesting either that virus components and associated host machinery can assemble in a space-limited environment and/or that the morphology of HIV-1–infected cells is dynamic.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the observation of virions budding from narrow regions of cytoplasm.

claim: The finding of budding virions along the plasma membrane of virus-producing cells that were not in direct contact with other cells suggested that the release of free virions from the plasma membrane is an in vivo HIV-1 dissemination mechanism.
source: The finding of budding virions along the plasma membrane of virus-producing cells that were not in direct contact with other cells (common in BM due to its low cell density) suggested that the release of free virions from the plasma membrane is an in vivo HIV-1 dissemination mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference from electron tomography imaging data.

claim: HIV-1 virions budding from the surface of virus-producing cells in bone marrow often showed a series of 2-4 thin, but electron-dense, bands that circumscribed the constricting bud neck.
source: HIV-1 virions budding from the surface of virus-producing cells in the BM often showed a series of 2–4 thin, but electron-dense, bands that circumscribed the constricting bud neck (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Immuno-electron microscopy demonstrated that the CHMP1B and CHMP2A ESCRT-III proteins are present at locations in budding virions where bands of electron density form.
source: We previously used immuno-EM to demonstrate that the CHMP1B and CHMP2A ESCRT-III proteins are present at locations in budding virions where these bands of electron density form (Ladinsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The location of the bands within the bud neck is consistent with their identification as components of ESCRT-III, which transiently polymerize into spirals at the necks of budding virions to facilitate plasma membrane abscission and virus release.
source: In addition, the location of the bands within the bud neck is consistent with their identification as components of ESCRT-III, which transiently polymerize into spirals at the necks of budding virions to facilitate plasma membrane abscission and virus release (Sundquist and Krausslich, 2012) (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and imaging data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The resemblance of the bands to electron microscopy structures of polymerized ESCRT-III proteins and similarity to a 'dome' model of ESCRT-mediated membrane scission further suggests that the bands represent polymerized ESCRT-III spirals.
source: Finally, their resemblance to EM structures of polymerized ESCRT-III proteins and similarity to a 'dome' model of ESCRT-mediated membrane scission (Schöneberg et al., 2017; Sundquist and Krausslich, 2012) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) further suggests that the bands represent polymerized ESCRT-III spirals (Johnson et al., 2018; McCullough et al., 2015; McCullough et al., 2018; Sundquist and Krausslich, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Putative ESCRT-III densities were present only during a stage in the budding process when the bud neck was ~50-80% of the diameter of the budding virion itself.
source: In surveys of HIV-1 budding profiles emanating from virus-producing BM cells we confirmed that putative ESCRT-III densities were present only during a stage in the budding process when the bud neck was ~50–80% of the diameter of the budding virion itself (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The bands were not present when the bud neck was larger or smaller than 50-80% of the budding virion diameter, corresponding to earlier or later budding stages, respectively.
source: The bands were not present when the bud neck was larger or smaller than that ratio, corresponding to earlier or later budding stages, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The observation that the putative ESCRT-III densities are only present on buds that have relatively thick necks suggests that the presence of ESCRT-III spirals connotes a transient, and specific, temporal stage in the HIV-1 budding process.
source: Although ET of tissue samples produces a series of static images, we can use surveys of budding profiles to deduce aspects of a dynamic process such as budding. For example, the observation that the putative ESCRT-III densities are only present on buds that have relatively thick necks suggests that the presence of ESCRT-III spirals connotes a transient, and specific, temporal stage in the HIV-1 budding process.
evidence: This is an inference from electron tomography imaging data.

claim: The suggestion that ESCRT-III spirals connote a transient stage in HIV-1 budding is consistent with recent TIRF microscopy studies showing ESCRT-III accumulation at a specific stage of HIV-1 Gag accumulation and membrane closure prior to membrane constriction.
source: This suggestion is consistent with recent TIRF microscopy studies of individual budding viruses showing ESCRT-III accumulation at a specific stage of HIV-1 Gag accumulation and membrane closure prior to membrane constriction (Johnson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Virus-producing T-cells in bone marrow often showed numerous nascent virions budding from multiple sites along the plasma membrane.
source: Virus-producing T-cells in BM often showed numerous nascent virions budding from multiple sites along the plasma membrane (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The nascent virions represent simultaneous budding events.
source: Because our ET images represent snapshots of specific time points in the budding process captured by rapid fixation, we infer that the nascent virions represent simultaneous budding events.
evidence: This is an inference from electron tomography imaging data.

claim: All buds on a given virus-producing cell had similar neck diameters, and all either showed or did not show presumptive ESCRT-III bands.
source: In such cases, ET showed that all buds on a given cell had similar neck diameters, and that all either showed or did not show presumptive ESCRT-III bands.
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data.

claim: A virus-producing bone marrow T-cell was found to have six budding profiles on its surface within a 400 nm thick section.
source: For example, a virus-producing BM T-cell was found to have six budding profiles on its surface within a 400 nm thick section (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Electron tomography of each bud on a virus-producing bone marrow T-cell showed a similar neck diameter and presumptive ESCRT-III bands circumscribing each bud neck.
source: ET of each bud showed a similar neck diameter and presumptive ESCRT-III bands circumscribing each bud neck.
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data.

claim: All virions budding from a virus-producing bone marrow T-cell were at a similar stage of egress at the time the bone marrow sample was fixed.
source: These observations suggest that all virions budding from this cell were at a similar stage of egress at the time the BM sample was fixed
evidence: This is an inference from electron tomography imaging data.

claim: Release of virus from virus-producing T-cells in bone marrow occurs in a coordinated or synchronous fashion.
source: supporting the hypothesis that release of virus from virus-producing T-cells in BM occurs in a coordinated or synchronous fashion (Ladinsky et al., 2014)
evidence: This is an inference from electron tomography imaging data and is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: HIV-1 virions were found associated with, and budding from, the plasma membranes of large uropods that projected from T-cells and contacted nearby cells.
source: HIV-1 virions were found associated with, and budding from, the plasma membranes of large uropods that projected from T-cells and contacted nearby cells (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: One or two uropods were typically seen per cell.
source: One or two uropods were typically seen per cell.
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data.

claim: Uropod plasma membranes usually displayed numerous caveolae-like invaginations.
source: Uropod plasma membranes usually displayed numerous caveolae-like invaginations (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Caveolae-like invaginations on uropod plasma membranes imply that uropods are an active zone for endocytosis and signaling.
source: implying that uropods are an active zone for endocytosis and signaling (Cheng and Nichols, 2016; Sánchez-Madrid and Serrador, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference from electron tomography imaging data and is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The uropod mode of cell-to-cell contact contrasted with the common contact mode of macrophages, in which numerous pseudopods emanating from a macrophage surface engaged with multiple neighboring cells, sometimes enveloping entire cells.
source: The uropod mode of cell-to-cell contact contrasted with the common contact mode of macrophages, in which numerous pseudopods emanating from a macrophage surface engaged with multiple neighboring cells, sometimes enveloping entire cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Electron tomography and 3D modeling of a zone-of-contact between a T-cell uropod and a potential target cell showed a region between two uropod processes that included electron-dense material into which a virion was budding.
source: ET and 3D modeling of a zone-of-contact between a T-cell uropod and a potential target cell showed a region between two uropod processes that included electron-dense material into which a virion was budding (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: Mature virions were found within plasma membrane invaginations of virus-producing cells that were contacting potential target cells.
source: Mature virions were also found within plasma membrane invaginations of virus-producing cells that were contacting potential target cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Uropods actively facilitate the direct transfer of virions between virus-producing cells and target cells across a virological synapse.
source: Cumulatively, these observations describe a potential mechanism for virus dissemination in the BM by which uropods actively facilitate the direct transfer of virions between virus-producing cells and target cells across a virological synapse
evidence: This is an inference from electron tomography imaging data.

claim: A virological synapse is defined as a region of close proximity between a donor cell and a potential target cell, often including zones of direct contact, that facilitates transfer of material from the donor cell to the target cell.
source: which we define as a region of close proximity between a donor cell and a potential target cell, often including zones of direct contact, that facilitates transfer of material from the donor cell to the target cell.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors.

claim: Bone marrow macrophages identified by hCD68 labeling associated with HIV-1 p24 were detected by immunofluorescence microscopy.
source: BM macrophages (identified by hCD68 labeling) associated with HIV-1 p24 were detected by IF microscopy (Figure 1)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Bone marrow macrophages are characterized by having large populations of endocytic compartments, phagosomes and numerous morphologically-complex invaginations of the cell surface.
source: BM macrophages are characterized by having large populations of endocytic compartments, phagosomes and numerous morphologically-complex invaginations of the cell surface (Sewald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Both bone marrow macrophages and neutrophils in bone marrow from BLT humanized mice were polymorphonuclear.
source: Although both BM macrophages and neutrophils in BM from BLT hu-mice were indeed polymorphonuclear
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy imaging data.

claim: Neutrophils can be easily distinguished from macrophages by their smaller size and populations of large, evenly dense granules.
source: neutrophils can be easily distinguished from macrophages by their smaller size and populations of large, evenly dense granules.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell morphology.

claim: Neutrophils lack extensive, pleomorphic surface invaginations that are common to macrophages and are often enhanced after infection by HIV-1.
source: Furthermore, neutrophils lack extensive, pleomorphic surface invaginations that are common to macrophages and are often enhanced after infection by HIV-1 (Deneka et al., 2007; Graziano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Surface invaginations appeared electron-lucent in bone marrow macrophages.
source: Such invaginations appeared electron-lucent in BM macrophages (Figure 2; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy imaging data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Electron tomography showed several modes of bone marrow macrophages associated with HIV-1 virions, including phagosomes containing ingested virus-producing cells, virions budding from the cell surface, virions contained within small intracellular compartments in the cytoplasm, and virions contained within surface invaginations.
source: Cumulatively, ET showed several modes of BM macrophages associated with HIV-1 virions, including phagosomes containing ingested virus-producing cells (Figure 5), virions budding from the cell surface (Figure 3C,D), virions contained within small intracellular compartments in the cytoplasm (Figure 6), and virions contained within surface invaginations (Figure 7; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figures 3C,D, 5, 6, 7, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bone marrow macrophages that did not contain HIV-1 virions outnumbered macrophages associated with virions by ~20:1.
source: We estimate BM macrophages (as identified morphologically) that did not contain HIV-1 virions outnumbered macrophages associated with virions by ~20:1.
evidence: This is an estimate based on electron tomography imaging data.

claim: Montaged projection electron microscopy overviews revealed bone marrow macrophages in the process of phagocytosing T-cells.
source: Montaged projection EM overviews revealed BM macrophages in the process of phagocytosing T-cells (Figure 5)
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Electron tomography often showed mature and immature free HIV-1 virions within macrophage phagosomes alongside engulfed cells at varying degrees of degradation.
source: ET often showed mature and immature free HIV-1 virions within macrophage phagosomes alongside engulfed cells at varying degrees of degradation.
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data.

claim: Classification of free virions as mature or immature was based upon the presence of a cone-shaped core (mature) or incomplete 'C-shaped' core (immature).
source: Classification of free virions as mature or immature was based upon the presence of a cone-shaped core (mature) (Figure 5B,D; upper right inset) or incomplete 'C-shaped' core (immature) (Figure 5D; lower left inset).
evidence: This describes the method for classifying virions and is shown in Figure 5B,D.

claim: Virions were found in early endosomal compartments adjacent to and/or continuous with the phagosome.
source: Virions were also found in early endosomal compartments adjacent to and/or continuous with the phagosome (Figure 5C,D)
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The presence of virions in early endosomal compartments adjacent to and/or continuous with the phagosome suggests a pathway for transfer of HIV-1 from ingested T-cells into a macrophage.
source: suggesting a pathway for transfer of HIV-1 from ingested T-cells into a macrophage.
evidence: This is an inference from electron tomography imaging data.

claim: Previous studies of cultured macrophages and cells within gut-associated lymphoid tissue described intracellular virus-containing compartments that were continuous with thin channels that allowed direct access to the extracellular space.
source: Previous studies of cultured macrophages and cells within GALT described intracellular virus-containing compartments, but these were continuous with thin channels that allowed direct access to the extracellular space (Bennett et al., 2009; Deneka et al., 2007; Ladinsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: This study detected a class of compartments that were fully enclosed and showed no steady-state continuity with extracellular space.
source: In contrast, this current study detected a class of compartments that were fully enclosed and showed no steady-state continuity with extracellular space.
evidence: This is a primary finding from electron tomography experiments.

claim: Tomography and 3D modeling of enclosed compartments and the adjacent cellular volume demonstrated a clearly-distinguishable continuous membrane surrounding the compartment in all dimensions, with no association with other structures that linked them to extracellular space.
source: Tomography and 3D modeling of these compartments and the adjacent cellular volume demonstrated a clearly-distinguishable continuous membrane surrounding the compartment in all dimensions, with no association with other structures that linked them to extracellular space (Figure 6A,B; Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—video 1.

claim: HIV-1 virions were observed assembling at, budding into, and maturing within enclosed compartments.
source: HIV-1 virions were observed assembling at, budding into, and maturing within these compartments (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Enclosed compartments containing virions were distinguished from pleomorphic surface invaginations by the electron densities of their respective lumens.
source: Enclosed compartments containing virions were distinguished from pleomorphic surface invaginations by the electron densities of their respective lumens because the content of the enclosed compartments was denser and thereby appeared darker by EM (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The lumens of invaginations were mostly devoid of electron dense content and appeared comparatively lighter.
source: By contrast, the lumens of invaginations were mostly devoid of electron dense content and appeared comparatively lighter (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: The increased density of enclosed compartments likely resulted from retained biomolecules that were otherwise lost by fluid exchange from compartments with access to the extracellular space during tissue fixation.
source: The increased density of enclosed compartments likely resulted from retained biomolecules that were otherwise lost by fluid exchange from compartments with access to the extracellular space during tissue fixation.
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of the observed electron density differences.

claim: Tomography of bone marrow macrophages confirmed that compartments with lighter lumens were continuous with the cell periphery and therefore open to extracellular space.
source: Tomography of BM macrophages confirmed that compartments with lighter lumens were continuous with the cell periphery and therefore open to extracellular space (Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 6—video 2.

claim: Electron tomography more frequently revealed examples of virions budding into completely-enclosed compartments with dark lumens than virions budding from the plasma membranes of bone marrow macrophages.
source: Although virions were observed budding from the plasma membranes of BM macrophages (Figure 3C,D), ET more frequently revealed examples of virions budding into completely-enclosed compartments with dark lumens (Figure 7B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figures 3C,D, 7B, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Previous studies in cultured cells demonstrated that HIV-1 buds into internal regions of membrane contiguous with the plasma membrane rather than into endocytic compartments.
source: These results contrast with previous studies in cultured cells demonstrating that HIV-1 buds into internal regions of membrane contiguous with the plasma membrane rather than into endocytic compartments (Gaudin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: An enclosed compartment with a dark lumen containing a mature virus particle was observed in the process of fusing with a surface-accessible compartment with a lighter lumen.
source: In an example demonstrating that budding into an enclosed intracellular compartment could result in eventual virus release from a macrophage, an enclosed compartment with a dark lumen containing a mature virus particle was observed in the process of fusing with a surface-accessible compartment with a lighter lumen (Figure 6C; Figure 6—video 3)
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—video 3.

claim: The fusion of an enclosed compartment with a surface-accessible compartment suggests a pathway by which intracellular viruses can access and subsequently disseminate into extracellular space.
source: suggesting a pathway by which intracellular viruses can access and subsequently disseminate into extracellular space.
evidence: This is an inference from electron tomography imaging data.

claim: A large volume of a polymorphonuclear bone marrow macrophage (5.5 μm x 5.5 μm x 1.5 μm) was imaged by electron tomography.
source: In order to classify HIV-1 virions associated with enclosed compartments, a large volume of a polymorphonuclear BM macrophage (5.5 μm x 5.5 μm x 1.5 μm) was imaged by ET (Figure 7).
evidence: This describes the experimental method and is shown in Figure 7.

claim: Within a large volume of a polymorphonuclear bone marrow macrophage, virions were classified as either budding into enclosed compartments, free immature virions in enclosed compartments, mature virions in enclosed compartments, or mature virions in surface invaginations.
source: Within this volume, we classified virions as either budding into enclosed compartments, free immature virions in enclosed compartments, mature virions in enclosed compartments, or mature virions in surface invaginations (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This describes the experimental method and is shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: A large volume of a virus producing macrophage revealed 357 virions (budding, immature, and mature) located within intracellular locations.
source: This volume revealed 357 virions (budding, immature, and mature) located within intracellular locations of a virus producing macrophage.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of electron tomography imaging data.

claim: The large number (98) of observed budding virions suggested prolific budding into enclosed compartments.
source: The large number (98) of observed budding virions suggested prolific budding into enclosed compartments.
evidence: This is an inference from quantitative analysis of electron tomography imaging data.

claim: The number of free mature virions within enclosed compartments outnumbered free immature virions (216 versus 17), suggesting rapid maturation.
source: The number of free mature virions within enclosed compartments outnumbered free immature virions (216 versus 17), suggesting rapid maturation.
evidence: This is an inference from quantitative analysis of electron tomography imaging data.

claim: Relatively few mature virions (8) were found within surface-accessible invaginations, suggesting that the transfer of virions by fusion of enclosed compartments with surface invaginations is infrequent and slow.
source: Relatively few mature virions (8) were found within surface-accessible invaginations, suggesting that the transfer of virions by fusion of enclosed compartments with surface invaginations is infrequent and slow.
evidence: This is an inference from quantitative analysis of electron tomography imaging data.

claim: Light and electron microscopy of HIV-1-infected cultured cells have revealed important insights into the HIV-1 life cycle and mechanisms of virus transmission.
source: Light and electron microscopy of HIV-1–infected cultured cells have revealed important insights into the HIV-1 life cycle and mechanisms of virus transmission (Bennett et al., 2009; Bracq et al., 2017; Deneka et al., 2007; Folks et al., 1988; Martin et al., 2010; Sougrat et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cultured cells cannot replicate complex interactions encountered in vivo by viruses in the context of functioning immune cell populations within tissues.
source: but cultured cells cannot replicate complex interactions encountered in vivo by viruses in the context of functioning immune cell populations within tissues.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of cultured cell models.

claim: Imaging of HIV-1-infected lymphoid tissues is establishing the importance of tissues in virus dissemination, with each tissue providing insights into HIV-1 pathogenesis.
source: Imaging of HIV-1–infected lymphoid tissues is establishing the importance of tissues in virus dissemination, with each tissue providing insights into HIV-1 pathogenesis (Carias et al., 2013; Kieffer et al., 2017a; Kieffer et al., 2017b; Ladinsky et al., 2014; Law et al., 2016; Li et al., 2005; Murooka et al., 2012; Reinhart et al., 1997; Sewald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HIV-1 infection of bone marrow cells can cause hematopoietic defects.
source: HIV-1 infection of BM cells can cause hematopoietic defects (Alexaki and Wigdahl, 2008; Allen and Dexter, 1984; Folks et al., 1988; Mandell et al., 1995; Redd et al., 2007; Thiebot et al., 2001; Yamakami et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Relatively little is known about mechanisms of HIV-1 dissemination in bone marrow and their influence on downstream aspects of disease.
source: yet relatively little is known about mechanisms of HIV-1 dissemination in BM and their influence on downstream aspects of disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: High-resolution electron tomography imaging studies required extraction of bone marrow by direct removal from a long bone, which is not a possible sample preparation method from living humans or non-human primates.
source: Although directly-comparative imaging of infected human or NHP BM would be an informative addition to our study, we note that the high-resolution ET imaging studies described here required extraction of BM by direct removal from a long bone (see Materials and methods), which is not a possible sample preparation method from living humans or NHPs.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the experimental method.

claim: Bone marrow can be extracted from living subjects using needle aspiration, but in direct comparisons of macaque bone marrow extracted by needle aspiration versus removal from a long bone, physiologically-relevant regions distinct from mature red blood cells could not be located in the needle aspiration samples because they contained contaminating blood from the vasculature introduced during the procedure.
source: BM can be extracted from living subjects using needle aspiration, but in direct comparisons of macaque BM extracted by needle aspiration versus removal from a long bone, we could not locate physiologically-relevant regions that were distinct from mature red blood cells in the needle aspiration samples because they contained contaminating blood from the vasculature introduced during the procedure (M.S.L and P.J.B., unpublished observations).
evidence: This is based on unpublished experimental observations.

claim: The imaging studies in BLT humanized mouse bone marrow provided structural insights into mechanisms of HIV-1 dissemination in bone marrow and potentially other tissues.
source: Nonetheless, the imaging studies in BLT hu-mouse BM provided structural insights into mechanisms of HIV-1 dissemination in BM and potentially other tissues
evidence: This is a summary statement about the findings of the study.

claim: Many cell types permissive to HIV-1 reside in bone marrow, including CD4+ T-cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells.
source: Many cell types permissive to HIV-1 reside in BM, including CD4+ T-cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells (Alexaki and Wigdahl, 2008; Allen and Dexter, 1984; Folks et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CD4+ T-cells make up the largest lymphocyte subset in human bone marrow.
source: CD4+ T-cells make up the largest lymphocyte subset in human BM (Oetjen et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Reduction of CD4+ T-cell levels in bone marrow is associated with many infections and cancers.
source: and reduction of CD4+ T-cell levels in BM is associated with many infections and cancers (Di Rosa and Pabst, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Monocyte/macrophages make up a substantial cellular component of human bone marrow and are integral for tissue homeostasis, hematopoietic stem cell maintenance, and immune surveillance.
source: Monocyte/macrophages also make up a substantial cellular component of human BM and are integral for tissue homeostasis, HSC maintenance, and immune surveillance (Kaur et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Virus-producing T-cells and macrophages were detected in HIV-1-infected BLT humanized mouse bone marrow as early as 5-10 days post-infection by immunofluorescence and electron microscopy.
source: We detected virus-producing T-cells and macrophages in HIV-1–infected BLT hu-mouse BM as early as 5–10 days PI by IF and EM
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and electron microscopy imaging data.

claim: The timeframe of 5-10 days for detecting virus-producing cells in bone marrow is similar to that detected in non-human primate bone marrow.
source: a timeframe similar to that detected in NHP BM (Mandell et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research in non-human primates.

claim: Light microscopy of bone marrow from HIV-1-infected humanized mice revealed hCD4+ T-cell depletion over time.
source: Additionally, light microscopy of BM from HIV-1–infected hu-mice revealed hCD4+ T-cell depletion over time.
evidence: This is supported by light microscopy imaging data.

claim: The results of hCD4+ T-cell depletion in humanized mouse bone marrow are consistent with non-human primate studies and human patients with AIDS.
source: These results are consistent with NHP studies (Hoang et al., 2019) and human patients with AIDS (Harris et al., 1990), which together support the use of hu-mice as a model to probe mechanisms of HIV-1 dissemination in BM.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in non-human primates and human patients.

claim: Vascularization supporting migration of cells to and from bone marrow, combined with trafficking of HIV-1-permissive cells, could be responsible for the rapid seeding of bone marrow with virus-producing cells detected by electron tomography.
source: Vascularization supporting migration of cells to and from BM (e.g., see Figure 2A), combined with trafficking of HIV-1–permissive cells, could be responsible for the rapid seeding of this tissue with virus-producing cells detected by ET.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Migration of HIV-1-infected cells to and from bone marrow is a potential mechanism for virus dissemination to lymphoid tissues throughout the body.
source: Because many immune cell types in BM are permissive to HIV-1 and can potentially migrate to other lymphoid tissues to take up permanent tissue residence (Alexaki and Wigdahl, 2008; Gorantla et al., 2006), we speculate that migration of HIV-1–infected cells to and from BM is a potential mechanism for virus dissemination to lymphoid tissues throughout the body.
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Studies in non-human primates showed increased levels of monocyte/macrophages released from bone marrow upon infection with SIV/SHIV.
source: Studies in NHPs showed increased levels of monocyte/macrophages released from bone marrow upon infection with SIV/SHIV (Hasegawa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research in non-human primates.

claim: Seeding of distant lymphoid tissue sites with virus-producing cells could enhance virus production and systemic spread early during HIV-1 infection.
source: This scenario would allow seeding of distant lymphoid tissue sites with virus-producing cells to enhance virus production and systemic spread early during HIV-1 infection.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the potential consequences of cell migration.

claim: Fewer virus-producing cells were found in bone marrow throughout the duration of the infection as compared to virus-producing cells from infected humanized mouse gut-associated lymphoid tissue at similar time points.
source: Although virus-producing cells were detected in BM within 5 days after infection, fewer such cells were found in BM throughout the duration of the infection as compared to virus-producing cells from infected hu-mouse GALT at similar time points (Kieffer et al., 2017b; Ladinsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with data from previous research.

claim: The lower density of virus-producing cells in bone marrow could be due to the lower reported density of T-cells in bone marrow (1-3%) as compared with that of gut-associated lymphoid tissue of humanized mice (~6%) or of human patients (~13%).
source: This could be due to the lower reported density of T-cells in BM (1–3%) (Bonomo et al., 2016; Monteiro et al., 2005) as compared with that of GALT of hu-mice (~6%) (Kieffer et al., 2017b) or of human patients (~13%) (McElrath et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Immunofluorescence and electron microscopy analysis of bone marrow revealed hCD68+ macrophages as a major cell population producing HIV-1 p24.
source: IF and EM analysis of BM revealed hCD68+ macrophages as a major cell population producing HIV-1 p24 (Figures 1 and 3)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and electron microscopy imaging data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The finding that macrophages are a major cell population producing HIV-1 p24 in bone marrow parallels non-human primate studies showing monocytes/macrophages to be an early and important target of SIV in bone marrow.
source: which parallels NHP studies showing monocytes/macrophages to be an early and important target of SIV in BM (Kitagawa et al., 1991; Mandell et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research in non-human primates.

claim: Immunofluorescence revealed a sizeable population of p24+ cells that did not stain as hCD68+ or hCD4+.
source: IF revealed a sizeable population of p24+ cells that did not stain as hCD68+ or hCD4+ (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The sizeable population of p24+ cells that did not stain as hCD68+ or hCD4+ is consistent with CD4 downregulation by HIV-1-infected T-cells, or cell-free viruses.
source: consistent with CD4 downregulation by HIV-1–infected T-cells, or cell-free viruses.
evidence: This is an inference from immunofluorescence imaging data.

claim: An additional possibility is that the p24+ cells that did not stain as hCD68+ or hCD4+ represent CD4-/CD68- bone marrow myeloid suppressor cells, which were shown to be infected by SIV in vivo.
source: An additional possibility is this cell population represents CD4-/CD68- BM myeloid suppressor cells, which were shown to be infected by SIV in vivo (Sui et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: HIV-1 can be transmitted through infection by cell-free virus or through cell-to-cell contact, with the latter mechanism being more efficient in cultured cells.
source: HIV-1 can be transmitted through infection by cell-free virus or through cell-to-cell contact, with the latter mechanism being more efficient in cultured cells (Carr et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2007; Dimitrov et al., 1993; Jolly et al., 2004; Phillips, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In tissues, the prevalence and efficiency of cell-free versus cell-to-cell HIV-1 transmission mechanisms is less well understood, partly because of the complex and dynamic environment that HIV-1 encounters in the presence of an immune system and multiple cell types organized into tissues.
source: In tissues, the prevalence and efficiency of these two mechanisms of virus transmission is less well understood, partly because of the complex and dynamic environment that HIV-1 encounters the presence of an immune system and multiple cell types organized into tissues (Reviewed in Uchil et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Intravital imaging studies revealed cell-to-cell transmission of HIV-1 in tissues of humanized mice.
source: Intravital imaging studies revealed cell-to-cell transmission of HIV-1 in tissues of hu-mice (Murooka et al., 2012; Sewald et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The resolution of light microscopy makes it difficult to definitively assign virion fluorescence as representing cell-free versus cell-associated virions.
source: however, the resolution of LM makes it difficult to definitively assign virion fluorescence as representing cell-free versus cell-associated virions.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of light microscopy.

claim: Electron tomography was used to directly visualize cell-associated and cell-free virions within bone marrow during active HIV-1 infection in humanized mice.
source: In this study, we used ET to directly visualize cell-associated and cell-free virions within BM during active HIV-1 infection in hu-mice.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Examples of both cell-free and cell-associated virions were readily detected by electron tomography in bone marrow, suggesting that HIV-1 transmission in vivo can occur by both mechanisms.
source: One important observation from ET of BM was that examples of both cell-free and cell-associated virions were readily detected, suggesting that HIV-1 transmission in vivo can occur by both mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference from electron tomography imaging data.

claim: In previous electron tomography studies of more densely-packed cells in humanized mouse tissues such as gut-associated lymphoid tissue and spleen, examples of potential cell-to-cell spread of virions as well as abundant free virions were found.
source: In previous ET studies of more densely-packed cells in hu-mouse tissues such as GALT and spleen, we found examples of potential cell-to-cell spread of virions as well as abundant free virions (Kieffer et al., 2017b; Ladinsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The overall cell density in bone marrow is reduced compared to other lymphoid tissues.
source: Because the overall cell density in BM is reduced compared to other lymphoid tissues (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy imaging data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Virus-producing cells contacting other cells are more rare in bone marrow than in densely-packed tissues, but potentially more directed due to the lower density of cells.
source: we speculate that virus-producing cells contacting other cells are more rare in BM than in densely-packed tissues, but potentially more directed due to the lower density of cells.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed cell density.

claim: In contrast to previous electron tomography studies of HIV-1-infected BLT humanized mouse gut-associated lymphoid tissue, which revealed hundreds of mature virions localizing between cells, fewer cell-free virions were detected in humanized mouse bone marrow.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to our previous ET studies of HIV-1-infected BLT hu-mouse GALT, which revealed hundreds of mature virions localizing between cells (Ladinsky et al., 2014), we detected fewer cell-free virions in hu-mouse BM.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with data from previous research.

claim: The lower cell density of bone marrow compared with other tissues allows cell-free virus to more rapidly disseminate from virus-producing cells as opposed to being trapped in pools between densely-intercalated cells in gut-associated lymphoid tissue or spleen.
source: One interpretation for this difference is that the lower cell density of BM compared with other tissues allows cell-free virus to more rapidly disseminate from virus-producing cells as opposed to being trapped in pools between densely-intercalated cells in GALT or spleen (Kieffer et al., 2017b; Ladinsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Contrasting results between bone marrow and other tissues highlight the importance of tissue-specific characteristics (e.g., cell densities, cell populations, architecture, function) influencing HIV-1 transmission in different lymphoid tissues.
source: These contrasting results highlight the importance of tissue-specific characteristics (e.g., cell densities, cell populations, architecture, function) influencing HIV-1 transmission in different lymphoid tissues
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of results across different tissues.

claim: HIV-1 transmission does not occur by a singular mechanism in all tissues.
source: and that HIV-1 transmission does not occur by a singular mechanism in all tissues.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of results across different tissues.

claim: A striking observation revealed by electron tomography was the prevalence of bone marrow macrophages engulfing virus-producing cells, with examples at different stages of engulfment and degradation.
source: A striking observation revealed by ET was the prevalence of BM macrophages engulfing virus-producing cells, with examples at different stages of engulfment and degradation, demonstrating containment of intact, virus-producing cells in addition to individual virions within intracellular macrophage compartments (Figures 5–7; Figure 6—videos 1–3.
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figures 5-7 and Figure 6—videos 1-3.

claim: Macrophages in bone marrow actively engulfed and degraded T-cells that were producing virus and could represent an example in lymphoid tissue similar to results in cultured macrophages describing removal of virus-producing T-cells via efferocytosis.
source: These results suggested that macrophages in BM actively engulfed and degraded T-cells that were producing virus and could represent an example in lymphoid tissue similar to results in cultured macrophages describing removal of virus-producing T-cells via efferocytosis (phagocytic clearance of apoptotic cells) (Baxter et al., 2014; Chua et al., 2018)
evidence: This is an inference from electron tomography imaging data and is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The results of macrophages engulfing virus-producing T-cells are similar to reports of macaque macrophages containing phagocytosed SIV-infected CD4+ T-cells.
