source: and to reports of macaque macrophages containing phagocytosed SIV-infected CD4+ T-cells (DiNapoli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research in non-human primates.

claim: In vitro fluorescence microscopy and electron microscopy studies of HIV-1-infected human CD4+ T-cells cultured with uninfected human macrophages showed fusion of infected T-cells and macrophages to form multinucleated giant cells.
source: Our results also address in vitro fluorescence microscopy and EM studies of HIV-1–infected human CD4+ T-cells cultured with uninfected human macrophages that showed fusion of infected T-cells and macrophages to form multinucleated giant cells (Bracq et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Similar phenomena of macrophage-T-cell fusion were reported through electron microscopy analysis of human patient samples.
source: similar phenomena were also reported through EM analysis of human patient samples (Orenstein and Wahl, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Examples of macrophage-T-cell fusion were not observed in bone marrow, although many examples of macrophages ingesting cells resembling T-cells were found.
source: By contrast, we did not observe examples of macrophage–T-cell fusion, although we found many examples of macrophages ingesting cells resembling T-cells in BM.
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data.

claim: 3D imaging showed that macrophages that appeared to include multiple nuclei in individual immunofluorescence optical sections or electron microscopy projection images actually contained single, polymorphous nuclei with connections between individual nuclear lobes.
source: In addition, we showed by 3D imaging that macrophages that appeared to include multiple nuclei in individual IF optical sections or EM projection images actually contained single, polymorphous nuclei with connections between individual nuclear lobes (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by 3D imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Electron microscopy of macrophages in the process of engulfing cell(s) included the additional nuclei from the ingested cell itself, and electron tomography showed these nuclei to be physically separated from the nucleus and cytoplasm of the macrophage by a membrane-enclosed space.
source: However, EM of macrophages in the process of engulfing cell(s) included the additional nuclei from the ingested cell itself, and ET showed these nuclei to be physically separated from the nucleus and cytoplasm of the macrophage by a membrane-enclosed space (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Figure 5C shows a macrophage that completely engulfed two other cells, each delineated by intact membranes or phagosomes.
source: For example, Figure 5C shows a macrophage that completely engulfed two other cells, each delineated by intact membranes or phagosomes.
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: By light microscopy, a macrophage that completely engulfed two other cells could be interpreted as a single cell containing multiple distinct nuclei within the cytoplasm.
source: By light microscopy this could be interpreted as a single cell containing multiple distinct nuclei within the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is an inference about how light microscopy images could be misinterpreted.

claim: Bone marrow macrophages producing and harboring large numbers of virions within intracellular locations were detected.
source: We detected BM macrophages producing and harboring large numbers of virions within intracellular locations.
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data.

claim: In one example, 357 virions were detected within a 5.5 μm x 5.5 μm x 1.5 μm volume of a bone marrow macrophage.
source: In one example, 357 virions were detected within a 5.5 μm x 5.5 μm x 1.5 μm volume of a BM macrophage.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of electron tomography imaging data.

claim: Extrapolating the results to the approximate volume of the macrophage imaged (~2800 μm³) and subtracting half of the volume as nucleus not containing virions (~1400 μm³), an individual bone marrow macrophage could harbor >11,000 virions.
source: Macrophages are larger than T-cells and extrapolating these results to the approximate volume of the macrophage imaged (~2800 um3) and subtracting half of the volume as nucleus not containing virions (~1400 um3), an individual BM macrophage could harbor >11,000 virions.
evidence: This is an extrapolation from quantitative analysis of electron tomography imaging data.

claim: Virions harbored by bone marrow macrophages could represent a potential virus reservoir as macrophages are long-lived, motile, and frequently interact with target cells.
source: These virions could represent a potential virus reservoir as macrophages are long-lived, motile, and frequently interact with target cells.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the potential role of macrophages as a virus reservoir.

claim: Virus-containing intracellular compartments have been observed in cultured macrophages and in cells from gut-associated lymphoid tissue and spleen.
source: Virus-containing intracellular compartments have been observed in cultured macrophages (Bennett et al., 2009; Deneka et al., 2007) and in cells from GALT and spleen (Kieffer et al., 2017b; Ladinsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In previous cases, the apparently intracellular compartments were directly continuous with the extracellular space by means of thin channels.
source: However, in previous cases, the apparently intracellular compartments were directly continuous with the extracellular space by means of thin channels.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Examples of virus-containing intracellular compartments that were enclosed with no continuity with the extracellular space were found in bone marrow.
source: Here, we found examples of virus-containing intracellular compartments that were enclosed with no continuity with the extracellular space (Figure 6A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 6A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, and Figure 6—video 1.

claim: HIV-1 was observed budding into enclosed compartments and at different stages of maturation within them, suggesting that they serve as sites for virus assembly and associated host-cell derived budding machinery.
source: HIV-1 was observed budding into these compartments and at different stages of maturation within them, suggesting that they serve as sites for virus assembly and associated host-cell derived budding machinery.
evidence: This is an inference from electron tomography imaging data.

claim: The completely-enclosed compartments in bone marrow macrophages typically contained only 1-3 virions in the form of nascent buds, immature free virions, or mature free virions.
source: The completely-enclosed compartments in BM macrophages typically contained only 1–3 virions in the form of nascent buds, immature free virions, or mature free virions.
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data.

claim: The result that completely-enclosed compartments in bone marrow macrophages typically contained only 1-3 virions contrasts with virus-containing compartments in cultured macrophages and in cells within gut-associated lymphoid tissue and spleen tissue, which contained ≥20 (gut-associated lymphoid tissue and spleen) and ≥50 (cultured cells) virions.
source: This result contrasts with virus-containing compartments in cultured macrophages and in cells within GALT and spleen tissue, which contained ≥20 (GALT and spleen) and ≥50 (cultured cells) virions.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with data from previous research.

claim: Examples of fusion between a completely-enclosed compartment and a compartment with access to the extracellular space were observed, supporting a route by which viruses could be produced, stored, and released by macrophages in tissues.
source: Budding into a completely-enclosed intracellular compartment seems unproductive for a virus; however, we observed examples of fusion between a completely-enclosed compartment and a compartment with access to the extracellular space (Figure 6; Figure 6—video 3), supporting a route by which viruses could be produced, stored, and released by macrophages in tissues.
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography imaging data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—video 3.

claim: The studies reveal macrophages to be actively involved in HIV-1 dissemination in bone marrow.
source: Cumulatively, our studies reveal macrophages to be actively involved HIV-1 dissemination in BM
evidence: This is a summary statement about the findings of the study.

claim: Virus-producing bone marrow macrophages could support systemic virus spread to distant tissue locations as they differentiate into tissue-resident macrophages and migrate to distant lymphoid sites.
source: suggesting the intriguing possibility that virus-producing BM macrophages could support systemic virus spread to distant tissue locations as they differentiate into tissue-resident macrophages and migrate to distant lymphoid sites.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the potential role of bone marrow macrophages in systemic virus spread.

claim: The ability of bone marrow macrophages to produce and harbor virus early after infection could function as a virus reservoir with the potential to promote virus dissemination to distant tissue locations.
source: The ability of BM macrophages to produce and harbor virus early after infection could function as a virus reservoir with the potential to promote virus dissemination to distant tissue locations.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the potential role of bone marrow macrophages as a virus reservoir.
